title: A Proud Tyrant Brought Low
overview: Isaiah promises Israel's return from exile and mocks the downfall of Babylon's king, then warns that Assyria and the Philistines will fall too.

parts.label: Captives come home (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The LORD promises to settle Israel in its own land again, with foreigners joining them and their former captors becoming their servants. It pictures a complete turning of the tables after exile, though some later readers took it to mean nations won over rather than conquered.

parts.label: Earth and the dead mock (vv. 3-11)
parts.note: Freed from forced labor, Israel is to sing a mocking song over the king of Babylon, who is never named (scholars are unsure which ruler was first meant), and even the cedars he cut down for building and war celebrate his end. In the realm of the dead (Sheol in Hebrew), the ghosts of earlier kings rise from their thrones to jeer that he is now as weak as they are, with maggots for his bed.

parts.label: The fallen morning star (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: The king is mocked as the shining morning star, son of the dawn, who planned to climb above God's stars to the mountain where the gods met in the far north, only to be thrown down into the pit (translations differ here: some say 'the far north', others name the sacred mountain Zaphon). Many scholars hear an old Canaanite story here about a star that tried to rise too high, while early Christian writers linked these lines with Satan's fall, and the Latin word for morning star, Lucifer, later stuck as a name for the devil.

parts.label: No grave, no heirs (vv. 16-23)
parts.note: Onlookers stare at the man who shook kingdoms, now lying unburied among the battle dead because he ruined his own land and people, a deep disgrace when kings rested in honored tombs. The poem then calls for his sons to be killed for their ancestors' sins so his family never rules again, and the LORD vows to wipe out Babylon's name and leave the city a swamp for wild creatures.

parts.label: Assyria will be broken (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: The LORD swears that Assyria, the empire threatening Judah in Isaiah's own day, will be crushed on his mountains and its heavy yoke lifted from his people. Readers often link this with Assyria's failed siege of Jerusalem around 701 BC, told in chapters 36 and 37.

parts.label: Warning to the Philistines (vv. 28-32)
parts.note: Dated to the year King Ahaz died, this warns the Philistines not to celebrate that the rod that struck them is broken, because a deadlier snake will spring from its root. Scholars are unsure whether that rod was a king of Judah or of Assyria, and the Philistine envoys, perhaps seeking allies, are told that the LORD founded Zion and his suffering people will find refuge there.

disagreement: Many Christians, following early church writers, read verses 12 to 15 as also describing Satan's fall from heaven, while others, including most modern scholars and traditional Jewish interpreters, see only a taunt against a human king that was applied to Satan later.
think: When a cruel ruler finally falls, what makes celebrating feel right, and where, if anywhere, does it start to feel wrong to you?
